newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bourse to change minimum deal sizes.
newsitem.headline: German bourse to change minimum deal sizes.

text.p: The German stock exchange is to rework the minimum order sizes required for the IBIS electronic share dealing system from June 2, resulting in higher threshholds for many blue chip share orders.
The bourse said on Monday it would switch to a new calculation system for minimum order sizes which takes into account the traded value of a stock rather than just its par value.

That will affect 75 of the 108 shares traded on IBIS, with the minimum order size for many blue chips set to rise to 1,000 shares from the current 500-, or 100-unit thresholds, while a minority will see the order requirement fall.
The change corresponds with the wishes of market participants and will be compatible with Xetra, the new electronic trading system which is scheduled to replace IBIS this year, the bourse said.
Current exchange rules set a minimum order volume of 100 shares for all stocks with a par value of 50 marks and a minimum order volume of 500 shares for stocks with a five mark par value.
Under the new system, minimum volumes will range from 50 to 1,000 shares, depending on the share's price.
The expensively priced insurance company AMB Holding, for example, which was trading on Monday at 1,460 marks, will see its minimum order threshold fall to 50 shares from 100.
Carmaker BMW AG, which was trading at 1,460 marks on Monday, will also see its order threshold fall to 100 shares from 500.
Meanwhile airline Deutsche Lufthansa, whose minimum order volume is currently 100 shares, will see that threshold rise to 1,000 shares. Lufthansa was trading at 28.20 marks on Monday.

Fellow blue chips RWE AG, Veba AG, Hoechst AG, Deutsche Telekom AG, Deutsche Bank AG, Dresdner Bank AG, Bayerische Vereinsbank AG, Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel-Bank AG, BASF AG and Bayer AG will also have 1,000-share order minimums.
Many German shares have fallen in face value in recent years because of a trend to reduce their par value from 50 marks to five marks by means of the equivalent of a ten-for-one share split.
